deep.reconstruction:
PART A (continuing from the previous page): singular solutions of a first-order algebraic ODE.

Setting. F(x,y,y')=0 with F a polynomial; Hilbert reuses the letter f for both F and the solution. There is an analytic function y=f(x,c) of x and a parameter c, given locally by a power series P(x,c). Letting c run along arbitrary paths, i.e. continuing analytically in c, gives a family of solutions: the 'general integral'.

Method.
(i) Solve the c-discriminant condition ∂f/∂c(x,c)=0 for c as an analytic function c=φ(x).
(ii) Substitute to get y=f(x,φ(x)). Geometrically this is the envelope of the one-parameter family.
(iii) Keep only those curves that actually satisfy the ODE.

Claim. The general family together with these envelope solutions gives all solutions. Hilbert adds in parentheses '(all analytic solutions, or all solutions at all)', which shows he was unsure of the scope.

Why envelopes are solutions [my addition]. Along y=f(x,φ(x)) we have dy/dx = f_x + f_c·φ' = f_x, because f_c=0 there. So the envelope has, at each point, the same slope as the member of the family through that point. Hence it satisfies F=0 wherever the envelope is a genuine curve. The explicit check in step (iii) is still needed, because the c-discriminant can also contain cusp loci or nodal loci that are not solutions.

PART B: 'Klein's fundamental theorem' and its proof sketch (the proof is finished on the next page).

Statement.
- G is a finite group of linear substitutions of x1..xn.
- H is a group of linear substitutions of y1..ym, isomorphic to G via g ↦ h_g.
- Claim: there exist n polynomials φ1(y),...,φn(y) that are permuted/transformed under H exactly as x1..xn are under G. In modern terms, there is a polynomial G-equivariant map from the y-space to the x-space (a 'covariant' of type x).

Construction.
1. Introduce dual variables u1..un that transform with each substitution so that the form u1x1+...+unxn is preserved. In modern terms u is contragredient to x; Hilbert's 'u·x = 0 bleibt' is the projective way of saying this.
2. Choose a linear form ψ1(y) that is changed by every non-identity element of H. Such a form exists because each fixed subspace is proper and a finite union of proper subspaces cannot exhaust the space. [Justification mine.]
3. Transform the pair (u1, ψ1) simultaneously by all N=|G| elements of the group, giving N pairs (u1^(g), ψ^(g)).
4. Form the power sums S_k = Σ_g u1^(g)·(ψ^(g))^k for k=1,2,3,...

Why S_k works [completion mine, as on next page].
- Each S_k is invariant under the simultaneous action, since the sum runs over the whole group.
- S_k is linear in u.
- Write S_k = Σ_i u_i Φ_i^(k)(y). Then invariance of an expression linear in the contragredient u means the coefficients (Φ_1^(k),...,Φ_n^(k)) transform cogrediently with x. These coefficients are the sought φ1..φn.

Non-vanishing.
- Suppose S_1,...,S_N all vanished identically in u.
- Then the linear system Σ_g u1^(g)(ψ^(g))^k = 0 (k=1..N) would have a nontrivial solution vector (u1^(g))_g; each u1^(g) is a nonzero linear form.
- Its determinant det[(ψ^(g))^k] = Π_g ψ^(g) · Π_{g<g'}(ψ^(g') − ψ^(g)) would then have to vanish.
- But the ψ^(g) are pairwise distinct (by the choice of ψ1) and nonzero, so the determinant is a nonzero polynomial. Contradiction.
- Hence some S_h ≢ 0, and its u-coefficients give the equivariant polynomials, which are homogeneous of degree h.
errors: Part A: the claim that the general integral plus envelope curves gives 'all' solutions is stated without proof. Hilbert himself hedges ('alle analytischen Lösungen oder überhaupt alle'). Several points are glossed over: limit values of c (e.g. c→∞), branch-point behaviour of φ(x), and the fact that singular solutions come more naturally from the p-discriminant of F. The step 'keep those that satisfy the ODE' correctly filters out cusp and nodal loci.
Notation clash: f denotes both the polynomial ODE F(x,y,y') and the solution family y=f(x,c).

Part B: Hilbert calls the u-substitutions 'cogredient' to x, although keeping u1x1+...+unxn invariant makes them contragredient in standard (Clebsch-Gordan era) terminology. 'u·x = 0 bleibt' is a projective phrasing of that invariance.
Part B: 'bei keiner Substitution der H ungeändert' must mean no non-identity substitution, since the identity fixes every form.

Part B: tacit assumptions. G must be finite, and H must act faithfully, i.e. be a true isomorphism rather than a homomorphic image, so that distinct elements give distinct ψ^(g). The power range k must start at 0 or ψ^(g) must be nonzero (automatic for a nonzero form). The next page also switches the name ψ to φ.

results.what: Singular (envelope) solutions of an algebraic first-order ODE F(x,y,y')=0, obtained by eliminating c from ∂f/∂c=0 in the general integral y=f(x,c) and keeping the curves that satisfy the ODE; claimed completeness of the solution set.
results.modern_name: c-discriminant / envelope theory of singular solutions
results.usually_credited_to: Clairaut, Lagrange (18th c.); systematized by Cayley and Darboux (1870s)

results.what: For a finite linear group G on x and an isomorphic linear group H on y, there exist polynomials φ1..φn in y transforming like x1..xn.
results.modern_name: Existence of polynomial equivariants (covariants) for finite groups, a step in Klein's theory of form problems / resolvents
results.usually_credited_to: F. Klein (Vorlesungen über das Ikosaeder, 1884, and related papers on equations of degree 5 and 6)

results.what: Proof via the Reynolds-type sums Σ_g u^(g)(ψ^(g))^k over the group, with a generic linear form ψ; non-vanishing via the Vandermonde determinant.
results.modern_name: Averaging (Reynolds operator) plus Vandermonde/Lagrange-resolvent argument; essentially that the polynomial functions on a faithful representation contain every irreducible representation
results.usually_credited_to: Klein's school (Klein, Gordan); the Vandermonde trick goes back to Lagrange

deep.surprise_reason: Both items are lecture-notebook material. Part A is classical singular-solution theory. Part B is explicitly labelled 'Kleins Fundamentalsatz' and is a clean but standard averaging-plus-Vandermonde proof from Klein's circle, recorded around Hilbert's early (Königsberg) invariant-theory period. It is of interest only as documentation of Hilbert's study of Klein's work.
